Calendar line 1
Case Name: Villalobos Living Trust Dated January 9, 2019
Case No.: 22PR192748

INTRODUCTION
On June 22, 2022, Petitioners Maria Esther Gonzalez, Maria Teresa Villalobos, Rogelio
Villalobos, Ismael Villalobos Ramos, Maria Concepcion Villalobos Ramos, Antonia
Villalobos Ramos and Jorge Odilon Villalobos (collectively, “Petitioners”) initiated this action
by filing a petition to invalidate the Villalobos Living Trust dated January 9, 2019. Petitioners
are the siblings of Decedent trustor Juan Manuel Villalobos (“Decedent”) who are not
beneficiaries under the trust. They contend that two of their other siblings Respondents San
Juana Villalobos and Jose De Jesus Villalobos (collectively, “Respondents”), who are both
trustees and beneficiaries of the trust, procured the trust by undue influence, fraud and elder
abuse. They also assert that Decedent lacked capacity to execute the trust.
On November 12, 2025, after a successful motion to amend, Petitioners filed an
amended petition (“FAP”) in which they also seek to invalidate an alleged “amendment” to the
trust in the form of a letter from Decedent dated January 20, 2019 (the “Amendment”).1
On May 28, 2025, Respondents filed a response and objection to the FAP
(“Objection”).

On October 20, 2025, Petitioners filed a petition to disinherit Respondents pursuant to
the no contest clause in the original trust (“No Contest Petition”) based on the content of
Respondents’ Objection.

Currently before the court is Respondents’ anti-SLAPP motion targeting the No Contest
Petition. Petitioners have opposed the motion and Respondents have filed a reply.

DISCUSSION
I. Petitioners’ Request for Judicial Notice
Petitioners request judicial notice of the Objection, filed May 28, 2025. That request is
GRANTED pursuant to Evidence Code section 452, subdivision (d).2
1 Although the motion to amend was granted via written order on April 24, 2025 and
Respondents filed their Objection on May 28, 2025, the FAP was not filed until November 12,
2025.
2 While the text of the request for judicial notice asks the court to take judicial notice of the
Objection, it is not attached to the request for judicial notice. What is attached is Respondents’
objection to the no contest petition. Nonetheless, the court has considered the Objection as it
must to determine whether Petitioner’s No Contest Petition has the requisite minimal merit to
survive the anti-SLAPP motion.

II. Timeliness of the Motion
Petitioners contend that the motion is untimely and improper because the court denied
Respondent’s ex parte application to file an anti-SLAPP motion after the 60-day deadline. A
“special motion [to strike] may be filed within 60 days of the service of the complaint or, in the
court’s discretion, at any later time upon terms it deems proper. The motion shall be scheduled
by the clerk of the court for a hearing not more than 30 days after the service of the motion
unless the docket conditions of the court require a later hearing.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 425.16,
subd. (f).)
Here, Petitioners assert that the No Contest Petition was served on Respondents on
November 10, 2025. The motion was not filed until February 23, 2026, more than 60 days
later. On January 27, 2026, Respondents filed an ex parte application seeking the court’s
permission to file the anti-SLAPP motion. The court denied that request indicating, inter alia,
that the requisite showing of immediate harm had not been met. Petitioners overstate the effect
of the court’s order denying the ex parte application. The court did not prevent Petitioners from
filing their motion, it merely found that the ex parte application standard had not been met. The
court has discretion to consider an untimely anti-SLAPP motion. (See Code Civ. Proc., §
425.16, subd. (f).) The court will exercise its discretion to do so in this case.
III. Legal Background
Code of Civil Procedure section 425.16 provides a summary procedure by which
defendants may dispose of “strategic lawsuits against public participation” or “SLAPP”
lawsuits, i.e. lawsuits brought “primarily to chill the valid exercise of constitutional rights of
freedom of speech and petition for the redress of grievances.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 425.16,
subd. (a).) The moving party bears the initial burden to make a threshold showing that the
challenged cause of action arises from acts that were taken in furtherance of the defendant’s
right of petition or free speech under the U.S. Constitution or the California Constitution in
connection with a public issue. (Id., at subd. (b); see also Equilon Enterprises, LLC v.
Consumer Cause, Inc. (2002) 29 Cal. 4th 53, 67 (Equilon).) If such a showing is made, the
anti-SLAPP motion will be granted only where the opposing party fails to demonstrate a
probability of prevailing on the claim. (Code Civ. Proc., § 425.16, subd. (b)(1).)
“Resolution of an anti-SLAPP motion involves two steps. First, the defendant must
establish that the challenged claim arises from activity protected by section 425.16. [Citation.]
If the defendant makes the required showing, the burden shifts to the plaintiff to demonstrate
the merit of the claim by establishing a probability of success. We have described this second
step as a ‘summary-judgment-like procedure.’ [Citation.] The court does not weigh evidence or
resolve conflicting factual claims. Its inquiry is limited to whether the plaintiff has stated a
legally sufficient claim and made a prima facie factual showing sufficient to sustain a favorable
judgment. It accepts the plaintiff’s evidence as true, and evaluates the defendant’s showing
only to determine if it defeats the plaintiff’s claim as a matter of law. [Citation.] ‘[C]laims with
the requisite minimal merit may proceed.’ [Citation.]” (Baral v. Schnitt (2016) 1 Cal.5th
376, 384-385, footnote omitted (Baral).)
Explained differently, “[a]t the first step, the moving defendant bears the burden of
identifying all allegations of protected activity, and the claims for relief supported by them.
When relief is sought based on allegations of both protected and unprotected activity, the
unprotected activity is disregarded at this stage. If the court determines that relief is sought
based on allegations arising from activity protected by the statute, the second step is reached.
There, the burden shifts to the plaintiff to demonstrate that each challenged claim based on
protected activity is legally sufficient and factually substantiated. The court, without resolving
evidentiary conflicts, must determine whether the plaintiff’s showing, if accepted by the trier
of fact, would be sufficient to sustain a favorable judgment. If not, the claim is stricken.
Allegations of protected activity supporting the stricken claim are eliminated from the
complaint, unless they also support a distinct claim on which the plaintiff has shown a
probability of prevailing.” (Baral, supra, 1 Cal.5th at p. 396.)
IV. Merits of the Motion
A. First Step
The No Contest Petition asserts that Respondents violated the no contest clause by
filing their Objection. The filing of the Objection in the probate court is a protected activity
under section 425.16, subdivision (e). (See Urick v. Urick (2017) 15 Cal.App.5th 1182,
1194 [“petition alleging a violation of the no contest clause arises from a pleading filed with
the probate court and therefore is subject to the anti-SLAPP statute”].) Accordingly,
Respondents have met their burden at the first step of the anti-SLAPP analysis and the burden
shifts to Petitioners to show a probability of prevailing on their claim.
B. Second Step
“At the second step, the court, without resolving evidentiary conflicts, must determine
whether the plaintiff’s showing, if accepted by the trier of fact, would be sufficient to sustain a
favorable judgment. If not, the claim is stricken. Allegations of protected activity supporting
the stricken claim are eliminated from the complaint, unless they also support a distinct claim
on which the plaintiff has shown a probability of prevailing.” (Baral, supra, 1 Cal.5th at p.
396.) “To satisfy the second prong, ‘a plaintiff responding to an anti-SLAPP motion must “
‘state[ ] and substantiate[ ] a legally sufficient claim.’ ” [Citations.] Put another way, the
plaintiff “must demonstrate that the complaint is both legally sufficient and supported by a
sufficient prima facie showing of facts to sustain a favorable judgment if the evidence
submitted by the plaintiff is credited.” ‘ [Citation.] ‘[The court considers] “the pleadings,
and supporting and opposing affidavits ... upon which the liability or defense is based.” [Citation.]
However, we neither “weigh credibility, [nor] compare the weight of the evidence. Rather,
[we] accept as true the evidence favorable to the plaintiff [citation] and evaluate the
defendant’s evidence only to determine if it has defeated that submitted by the plaintiff as a
matter of law.” ‘ [Citation.]” (Oasis West Realty, LLC v. Goldman (2011) 51 Cal.4th 811,
820.)
“Thus, the second step of the anti-SLAPP analysis is a ‘summary-judgment-like
procedure at an early stage of the litigation.’ [Citation.] In this step, a plaintiff ‘need only
establish that his or her claim has “minimal merit” [citation] to avoid being stricken as a
SLAPP.’ [Citations.]” (Key v. Tyler (2019) 34 Cal.App.5th 505, 515.)
i. No Contest Clauses in General
“ ‘A no contest clause “essentially acts as a disinheritance device, i.e., if a beneficiary
contests or seeks to impair or invalidate the trust instrument or its provisions, the beneficiary
will be disinherited and thus may not take the gift or devise provided under the instrument.”
[Citation.] “The purpose of no contest clauses ‘is to discourage will contests by imposing a
penalty of forfeiture against beneficiaries who challenge the will.’” [Citation.] “In essence, a
no contest clause conditions a beneficiary’s right to take the share provided to that beneficiary
under such an instrument upon the beneficiary’s agreement to acquiesce to the terms of the
instrument. [Citation.] [¶] …” [Citation.]’ [Citation.]” (Urick v. Urick, supra, 15 Cal.App.5th
at p. 1192.)
“No contest clauses are valid in California and are favored by the public policies of
discouraging litigation and giving effect to the settlor’s expressed purposes. [Citation.]
Competing public policies, however, also exist. The court must strictly construe a no contest
clause because it works a forfeiture and may not be extended beyond its plainly intended
function. [Citation.]” (Aviles v. Swearingen (2017) 16 Cal.App.5th 485, 490.)
“Under the current law, a no contest clause will only be enforced against a pleading that
challenges certain property transfers, a creditor’s claim, or ‘[a] direct contest that is brought
without probable cause. (Prob. Code, § 21311, subd. (a)(1).)” (Urick v. Urick, supra, 15
Cal.App.5th at pp. 1193-1194.) “ ‘Contest’ means a pleading filed with the court by a
beneficiary that would result in a penalty under a no contest clause, if the no contest clause is
enforced. (Prob. Code, § 21310, subd. (a).) “ ‘Pleading’ means a petition, complaint, cross-
complaint, objection, answer, response, or claim.” (Prob. Code, § 21310, subd. (d).)
“ ‘Direct contest’ means a contest that alleges the invalidity of a protected instrument or
one or more of its terms, based on one or more of the following grounds: (1) Forgery. (2) Lack
of due execution. (3) Lack of capacity. (4) Menace, duress, fraud, or undue influence. (5)
Revocation of a will pursuant to Section 6120, revocation of a trust pursuant to Section 15401,
or revocation of an instrument other than a will or trust pursuant to the procedure for
revocation that is provided by statute or by the instrument. (6) Disqualification of a beneficiary
under Section 6112, 21350, or 21380.” (Prob. Code, § 21310, subd. (b).)
“For the purposes of this section, probable cause exists if, at the time of filing a contest,
the facts known to the contestant would cause a reasonable person to believe that there is a
reasonable likelihood that the requested relief will be granted after an opportunity for further
investigation or discovery.” (Prob. Code, § 21311, subd. (b).)
ii. Application to the Instant Case
Here, the No Contest Petition argues that Respondents violated the no contest clause
contained in the original trust dated January 9, 2019 via statements made in their Objection.
The no contest clause is contained in article 8.3 of the trust, which provides, in pertinent part,
“If, without probable cause (as defined by California Probate Code § 21311(b) or any successor
statute), any beneficiary of any trust created under this instrument, singularly or in combination
with any other person or persons, files a direct contest (as defined by California Probate Code §
21310, or any successor statute) that alleges the invalidity of this instrument or one or more of
its terms or that alleges the invalidity of any will of the settlor or one or more of its
terms, which is in existence on the date this instrument is executed, then the right of that person
to take any interest given to him or her by this instrument shall be determined as it would have
been determined had the person predeceased the execution of this instrument without surviving
issue.” (See Verified Amended Petition to Invalidate Trust and Amendment, filed November
12, 2025, Ex. A.)3
The FAP asserts that the Amendment is invalid. Specifically, it states, “On or about
February 1, 2024, San Juana and Jose produced a trust amendment, Bates-stamped 000054,
purportedly signed by the Decedent on January 20, 2019 (which was eleven (11) days after the
initial Trust was executed) and prepared under direction of San Juana and her granddaughter,
Karla Inhary de Alba (‘Amendment’). . . . The Amendment . . . purports to distribute
Decedent’s Bank of America account and provide Karla with a tenancy of seven (7) years at
the Trust Property after his passing. It is San Juana’s attempt to grasp onto a family property
for her sole benefit and use, despite having already arranged for the Trust execution eleven
(11) days beforehand, and shows Respondents’ undue influence and fraud related to Decedent.
On July 18, 2024, during the deposition of Karla Inhary de Alba, who is San Juana’s
granddaughter, testified to transcribing Decedent’s dictation for the Amendment. Petitioners do
not believe it is a valid amendment to the Trust.” (FAP, ¶ 27.1.) The FAP goes on to allege that
Respondents procured the Amendment via undue influence, fraud, deceit, and concealment,
and that Decedent lacked capacity to execute it. (See FAP, ¶¶ 29, 30, 40, 41, 44, 61.)
Petitioners assert in the No Contest Petition that Respondent’s Objection to the FAP,
which itself seeks to invalidate both the original trust and the Amendment, constitutes a direct
trust contest because it argues for the validity of the Amendment. They maintain that the
defense of the allegedly invalid Amendment constitutes a contest of the terms of the original
trust because the Amendment effected a revocation of the original trust by stating terms
inconsistent with the original trust.

Petitioners rely primarily on Key v. Tyler (2019) 34 Cal.App.5th 505 (Key), in which
the Court of Appeal concluded that a trustee who defended a trust amendment she was found to
have obtained via undue influence violated the original trust’s no contest clause. (Id. at p. 523.)
In Key, two siblings disagreed over a 2007 amendment to a family trust. (Id. at p. 509.) Key
filed a petition alleging that her sister, Tyler, used undue influence to effectuate the
amendment. (Ibid.) The probate court issued a statement of decision granting the petition. (Id.
at p. 513.) After the Court of Appeal affirmed the probate court’s order, Key filed a petition to
enforce the trust’s no contest clause against Tyler on that ground that Tyler lacked probable
cause to defend the 2007 amendment. (Id. at pp. 509, 523-524.) Tyler responded by filing an
anti-SLAPP motion challenging Key’s no contest petition. (Id. at p. 513.) The probate court
granted the motion, concluding Key did not show a probability of success because she could
not establish Tyler lacked probable cause to defend the 2007 amendment. (Id. at pp. 513-514.)
The Court of Appeal reversed the probate code’s order denying the anti-SLAPP motion.
(Key, supra, 34 Cal.App.5th at p. 510.) The court explained that Tyler’s defense of the 2007
Amendment “clearly” fell within the scope of the trust’s no contest clause, which operated. As
to “ ‘specifically disinherit’ any ‘devisee, legatee or beneficiary’ who ‘contests either Trustor’s
Will, this Trust, any other trust created by a Trustor, or in any manner attacks or seeks to
impair or invalidate any of their provisions.’ By obtaining the 2007 Amendment through undue
influence and then defending that amendment in court, Tyler sought to ‘impair’ and
‘invalidate’ the provisions of the original Trust that the 2007 Amendment purported to
3 This petition is attached to Respondent’s counsel’s reply declaration and is present in the
record. Coincidentally, the trust instrument is not attached to the No Contest Petition.
replace.” (Id. at p. 523.) The court concluded that the defense of the 2007 amendment was a
direct contest because had it been successful, it would have had the effect of revoking the
portion of the trust it purported to replace. (Id. at p. 524.) That change would have revoked
Key’s right to inherit 33 1/3 percent of the estate and replaced it with a right to inherit “ ‘the
lesser of $1,000,000, or 5% of the then Survivor’s Trust Estate less any amount owed on any
outstanding promissory note in favor of the Surviving Trustor.’ ” (Ibid.)
The appellate court concluded Key showed a probability of prevailing on her no contest
petition because the probate court’s statement of decision contained factual findings, which the
court concluded amounted to admissible evidence Key could rely on to prove Tyler lacked
probable cause to defend the 2007 amendment. (See id. at pp. 534-539.) The court explained
the probate court’s findings supported an inference that “Tyler acted intentionally in
manipulating [the settlor] and in using ‘excessive persuasion’ on her to obtain terms in the
2007 Amendment that were not the result of [the settlor’s] free will.” (Id. at p. 538.) From this,
a court could find Tyler lacked probable cause because “a reasonable person in Tyler’s position
would not have believed there was a ‘reasonable likelihood’ that the 2007 Amendment was
valid.” (Id. at p. 539.)
Similarly, in Estate of Gonzalez (2002) 102 Cal.App.4th 1296 (Gonzalez), on which
Petitioners also rely, a beneficiary presented for probate a 1998 will that he had obtained from
his father through undue influence. (Id. at p. 1299.) The will purported to replace a 1992 will
containing a no contest clause. (Ibid.) After a trial at which the probate court found that the
1998 will was obtained via undue influence, the beneficiary’s sibling filed a no contest
petition, which the probate court granted. (Id. at p. 1302.) On appeal of that decision, the
appellate court concluded that, by offering the 1998 will to probate, the beneficiary brought a
“contest” seeking revocation because “the 1998 will revoked all prior wills, including the 1992
will with the no-contest clause.” (Id. at p. 1303.)
Here, in contrast to Key and Gonzalez, no prior finding of undue influence has been
made and the Amendment has not been invalidated. Thus, while defense of an invalid
amendment could constitute a trust contest, Petitioners must present evidence from which one
could conclude that the Amendment is invalid and that Respondents defend the Amendment in
a way that would violate the no contest clause.

Petitioners have failed to establish that the Amendment is at odds with the original trust
such that it would invalidate any provisions of the trust. Neither the No Contest Petition nor
Petitioner’s opposition to the instant anti-SLAPP motion mentions any provision of the trust
that would be invalidated by the Amendment, assuming that it was found the be valid. The No
Contest Petition states, “The Amendment purports to distribute Decedent’s Bank of America
account and provide Respondent Karla with a tenancy of 7 years at the Family Home after
Decedent’s passing.” (No Contest Petition, ¶ 3.) But, the No Contest Petition does not allege
that the Bank of America account or the home are trust assets. And, even assuming that the
home was a trust asset, the Amendment does not change the distribution of the home, the
Amendment states, “The house at 131 Milton Street, San Francisco CA 94112, as I have
already said to San Juana and Jesus, after I am gone, do not sell it until after seven years. I ask
this because I want Karla and her daughters to live there those seven years.” (Italics added.)
Thus, the Amendment does not change the beneficiaries entitled to receive the home,
Respondents would remain the beneficiaries. The Amendment simply added a restriction to
Respondents’ ability to sell the home.

As to the Bank of America account, the Amendment states, “Of the accounts I have
under my name an [sic] that of Teresa in Bank of America I want to add up all I have in the
checking and savings and distribute in the following manner: $20,000 to Teresa and $20,000 to
Esther as a thank you for their help taking care of my parents. $10,000 to Rogelio and $10,000
to Jorge and whatever is left, half for San Juana and the other half for Jesus.” To the extent the
Bank of America account is a trust asset, the above distribution would constitute a change from
the terms of the original trust, of which Respondents are the sole beneficiaries. Yet, Petitioners
do not provide any evidence that the Bank of America account is a trust account. Notably,
Decedent’s own description of the account suggests it is a joint account with one Petitioner.
Respondents take the position that the only trust asset is the home. (See Motion, ¶ 5.)
Petitioners argue that the Amendment has the effect of entirely revoking the trust. (See
Opposition, ¶ 12.) But, it could not do so. Probate Code section 15401, subdivision (a)
provides, “A trust that is revocable by the settlor or any other person may be revoked in whole
or in part by any of the following methods: (1) By compliance with any method of revocation
provided in the trust instrument. (2) By a writing, other than a will, signed by the settlor or any
other person holding the power of revocation and delivered to the trustee during the lifetime of
the settlor or the person holding the power of revocation. If the trust instrument explicitly
makes the method of revocation provided in the trust instrument the exclusive method of
revocation, the trust may not be revoked pursuant to this paragraph.”
Article 3 of the original trust states,
3.1 Power of Revocation and Amendment. Any trust created by this instrument
may be amended, revoked, or terminated by the settlor, in whole or in part, at
any time during his lifetime. After the settlor’s death, any trust created by this
instrument shall be irrevocable and not subject to amendment.
3.2. Method of Revocation or Amendment. Any amendment, revocation, or
termination of any trust created by this instrument shall be made by written
instrument, other than a will or codicil, that specifically refers to this trust
agreement and which is signed by the settlor and delivered to the trustee. An
exercise of the power of amendment substantially affecting the duties, rights,
and liabilities of the trustee shall be effective only if agreed to by the trustee in
writing. The written instrument for revocation or termination must specify that a
revocation or termination of trust is intended; a change in title or possession is
not sufficient for revocation or termination.

Under either the statutory revocation method or the method stated in the trust, the
Amendment would not be effective to revoke the trust because it states that it is a will, it does
not refer to the trust, and it does not specify that a revocation or termination of the trust is
intended. In fact, the Amendment states, “I Juan Manuel Villalobos want to say that this letter
is my will after I die.”4 While Respondents state in the Objection that the Amendment is valid,
4 The court notes that if the trust allows for revocation by will, such revocation is effective.
(Gardenhire v. Superior Court (2005) 127 Cal.App.4th 882, 894.) Here, however, the trust
does not allow revocation by will and the statutory method of revocation does not allow
revocation by will. Accordingly, to the extent the Amendment was an attempt at revocation, it
was not effective.
(see Objection, p. 2:14), they do not endorse a document that has the effect of revoking the
trust as Petitioners claim. Nor do they argue that the Amendment has or should have such an
effect. Thus, the instant case is distinguishable from Key and Gonzalez.
Finally, Petitioners present no evidence of undue influence by Respondents or evidence
that Decedent lacked capacity to execute the Amendment. Petitioners provide deposition
testimony of Respondent San Juana Villalobos in which she states that Decedent initially asked
her to transcribe the Amendment but that her granddaughter, Karla, ultimately did so.
(Declaration of John S. Rueppel in Support of Opposition [], Ex. A, pp. 84:7-9, 102:22-23.)
The deposition testimony also contains the following colloquy on which Petitioners rely:
Q. And that seven years is not -- is not in the trust he signed on January 10th;
correct?

A. No. He did it because -- he didn’t put it in the trust because Jesus argued that
he was going to live 100 and something years, that he couldn't put that in the
trust.· But I think the reason that Manuel did this letter or document is because
he wanted to protect my daughter and my granddaughter, for them to live
there…
This testimony does not suggest that Respondents contested the trust without probable cause.
Here, Petitioners have not even established in response to the anti-SLAPP motion that
the No Contest Clause has the requisite minimal merit to survive the motion. Accordingly, the
motion is GRANTED.

V. Requests for Attorney Fees
Code of Civil Procedure section 425.16, subdivision (c) provides that “a prevailing
defendant on a special motion to strike shall be entitled to recover that defendant’s attorney’s
fees and costs. If the court finds that a special motion to strike is frivolous or is solely intended
to cause unnecessary delay, the court shall award costs and reasonable attorney’s fees to a
plaintiff prevailing on the motion, pursuant to Section 128.5.”
Respondents request their fees as the prevailing parties but they do not request any
particular amount of fees, instead indicating an intent to file a memorandum of costs at a later
date. The court finds that Respondents are the prevailing parties on the anti-SLAPP motion and
are entitled to their reasonable attorney fees.

Petitioners request for fees is DENIED as they have not established that the motion was
frivolous or solely intended for the purposes of delay.

CONCLUSION
The anti-SLAPP motion is GRANTED. Respondents are awarded their fees.
Petitioners’ request for fees is DENIED.

IT IS SO ORDERED.
